target.title: fix(daemon): gateway fails to launch on Windows when the profile path contains CJK characters
target.body:
Closes #107416

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Windows users whose profile path contains CJK characters (e.g. `C:\Users\苗振`) can install OpenClaw but the gateway never starts: the first run fails with a "The system cannot find the file specified" / "找不到 …\gateway.vbs" popup and the Scheduled Task never launches the gateway. Reported against v2026.7.1 on Windows 11 with a Chinese-locale profile path.

## Why This Change Was Made

The daemon writes the generated launchers (`gateway.cmd`, the hidden `gateway.vbs` introduced by #95480, and the Startup-folder fallback entry) as UTF-8 without BOM, but neither Windows script host reads that encoding: `wscript.exe` parses `.vbs` only as ANSI or UTF-16 LE with BOM, and `cmd.exe` parses `.cmd` in the console (OEM) code page. CJK path bytes inside the launchers garble and the launch chain breaks at the first hop.

This PR adds `src/daemon/launcher-encoding.ts` — a per-format encoder plus a BOM-sniffing decoder — used at the three launcher write sites and the `readScheduledTaskCommand` parse site in `src/daemon/schtasks.ts`:

- `.vbs` → always UTF-16 LE with BOM, the one wscript encoding that is correct on every locale.
- `.cmd` → ASCII content stays byte-identical UTF-8 (zero change for non-CJK installs). Non-ASCII content is encoded with the system ANSI code page, but only on locales where ANSI == OEM (936/932/949/950/874/GB18030 — the locales where a code-page fix is well-defined). windows-125x locales keep UTF-8: their console OEM page (437/850/852/866…) differs from ANSI and has no WHATWG decoder, so ANSI bytes would just be a different flavor of wrong there. Encoded output is round-trip-verified with the same decoder the read path uses; unmappable characters fail the install with a clear error instead of writing a silently broken launcher.
- Read-back BOM-sniffs UTF-16, then tries strict UTF-8 first (covers ASCII and all pre-fix installs with no code page probe on the frequent poll path), then falls back to the ANSI code page — so repair/update parses legacy files fine and rewrites the state-dir launchers in the new encodings.

**Design notes:**

- **Why not UTF-16 for `.cmd`:** `cmd.exe` cannot parse UTF-16 batch files (NUL bytes break the parser).
- **Why iconv-lite:** encoding to GBK/Big5/… is required and `TextDecoder` only decodes. `iconv-lite@0.7.2` is already in the dependency tree (`express` → `body-parser`/`raw-body`), so promoting it to a root dependency resolves to the already-locked version and adds no new packages — the `npm-shrinkwrap.json` delta is one line. If a no-new-root-dependency route is preferred, the alternative is keeping `.cmd` UTF-8 and prepending `@chcp 65001>nul`; that mutates the console code page for child processes and relies on cmd's re-read behavior, but I am happy to switch if maintainers prefer it.
- **Code page detection** reuses the existing cached `resolveWindowsSystemEncoding()` in `src/infra/windows-encoding.ts` (now exported); no new detection code.
- **Known sibling surface (explicit follow-up, not in this PR):** `src/infra/windows-task-restart.ts` writes its temp restart `.cmd` as UTF-8 with the same class of embedded paths, so the update-time restart path on CJK hosts needs the same treatment. Kept out to hold this PR to one concern; I can file the follow-up issue once this lands.

## User Impact

Windows users with CJK (or Thai) characters anywhere in their profile/state path can now install and start the gateway, and gateway repair/update migrates existing broken installs by rewriting the state-dir launchers. Users with pure-ASCII paths get byte-identical launcher files — no change at all.

## Evidence

- New unit coverage `src/daemon/launcher-encoding.test.ts` (12 tests: UTF-16 BOM output incl. a CJK path, ASCII byte-identity under a pinned code page, GBK round-trip, windows-125x gate, unrepresentable-character failure, legacy-UTF-8 and raw-GBK decode).
- Migration coverage in `schtasks.test.ts`: `readScheduledTaskCommand` parses both a legacy UTF-8 CJK script and a GBK-encoded script.
- Install-path coverage in `schtasks.install.test.ts`: the hidden `.vbs` launcher for a CJK profile path starts with `FF FE` and utf16le-decodes to the exact `Run """…""", 0, False` line; an unrepresentable env value fails the install with no launcher file written.
- Focused runs on Windows (Node 24.18, pnpm 11.2.2): launcher-encoding 12/12, schtasks + schtasks.install 48/48, schtasks.startup-fallback + service-env + windows-encoding 137/137; `oxlint` and `oxfmt` clean on changed files; `tsgo:core` and `tsgo:test:src` clean; `deps:shrinkwrap:root:check` reports current. (`schtasks.stop.test.ts` shows 4 failures on this host that reproduce identically on unmodified `main` — pre-existing and unrelated.)
- Real-machine smoke test on Chinese Windows 10 (ACP=OEMCP=936, the reporter's locale family): a `gateway.vbs`/`gateway.cmd` pair written under `%TEMP%\苗振\` with the new encoder launches via `cscript gateway.vbs` and the payload creates `proof.txt`; the same pair written the old way (plain UTF-8) fails with `gateway-old.vbs(1, 1) (null): The system cannot find the file specified.` — the exact reported symptom — and no proof file appears.

target.title: fix(memory): reject hex/exponent dreaming integer config strings
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where dreaming phase integer config fields silently accepted JavaScript-specific string forms (`0x10`, `1e3`, `2.5`) via `Number()` coercion. A user who wrote `"0x10"` for `phases.deep.limit` got a promotion limit of 16 instead of the shipped default 10.

The fix targets the `pluginValidation: "skip"` path used by `openclaw configure`, `openclaw doctor` migration, and config mutation flows. In these paths, AJV JSON Schema validation is intentionally skipped, so malformed integer strings bypass the manifest's `"type": "integer"` guard and reach the resolver directly. The normal config-loading path (AJV `"full"`) already rejects these strings — this fix closes the gap for skip-validation callers.

## Why This Change Was Made

Reuse the shared `parseStrictNonNegativeInteger` / `parseStrictPositiveInteger` helpers from `@openclaw/normalization-core/number-coercion`, which enforce `/^[+-]?\d+$/` — rejecting hex prefixes, exponent notation, and fractional dots at the contract level. Ordinary decimal strings (`"5"`) and numeric literals (`5`) keep working; malformed strings fall back to shipped defaults or omit optional fields.

Key design decisions:
- Delete the local `Number()`-based `normalizeNonNegativeInt` / `normalizeOptionalPositiveInt` entirely — no compat shims, no dual path
- `normalizeScore` (float scores 0–1) intentionally retains `Number()` — scores are not integers, and `Number("0.9")` is the correct parse
- The fix is a 2-line change per function (replace implementation body with shared helper call); the bulk of the diff is deleting the old 12-line bodies

Collision check: searched open PRs for `path:src/memory-host-sdk/dreaming.ts` — **0** competing PRs.

## User Impact

Malformed hex/exponent/fraction dreaming integer strings no longer silently change lookback windows, promotion limits, or token/timeout budgets. Valid decimal config is unchanged.

| Config field | Input | Before (`Number()`) | After (strict) | Default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `deep.limit` | `"0x10"` | 16 | **10** (fallback) | 10 |
| `deep.minRecallCount` | `"1e3"` | 1000 | **3** (fallback) | 3 |
| `deep.recencyHalfLifeDays` | `"1.5"` | 1 (floored) | **14** (fallback) | 14 |
| `deep.maxAgeDays` | `"0x20"` | 32 | **30** (fallback) | 30 |
| `deep.maxPromotedSnippetTokens` | `"1e2"` | 100 | **160** (fallback) | 160 |
| `deep.execution.maxOutputTokens` | `"0x40"` | 64 | **undefined** (omitted) | - |
| `deep.execution.timeoutMs` | `"1e4"` | 10000 | **undefined** (omitted) | - |
| `light.lookbackDays` | `"0x0a"` | 10 | **2** (fallback) | 2 |

## Verification

- Exact head: `b008cb8a2b92f1dfbd6abc4c62f30b65c11e36ff`
- `oxfmt --check src/memory-host-sdk/dreaming.ts src/memory-host-sdk/dreaming.test.ts` — passed.
- `oxlint src/memory-host-sdk/dreaming.ts src/memory-host-sdk/dreaming.test.ts` — passed; exit 0.
- `git diff --check` — passed; exit 0.
- Focused tests:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/memory-host-sdk/dreaming.test.ts -- --run
```

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  16 passed (16)
```

- Mutation check: `git checkout origin/main -- src/memory-host-sdk/dreaming.ts` → 11 proof assertions fail (hex/exponent silently coerced) → restore fix → 31/31 pass.

## Real behavior proof

### Behavior addressed

Two layers:
1. **Normal config-loading path (`pluginValidation: "full"`):** AJV JSON Schema validation with `"type": "integer"` already rejects string values — config load fails with `"must be integer"` errors. The fix here is defense-in-depth.
2. **Skip-validation path (`pluginValidation: "skip"`):** Used by `openclaw configure`, doctor migration, and config mutation flows. AJV is intentionally bypassed, so malformed strings like `"0x10"` survive validation and reach `resolveMemoryDreamingConfig` as raw strings. The old `Number()` path silently coerced these into wrong values; the fix rejects them and falls back to defaults.

The proof exercises both the `"full"` and `"skip"` validation paths via the real `validateConfigObjectWithPlugins` function, then feeds the skip-validated plugin config through the real `resolveMemoryDreamingConfig` resolver.

### Real env tested

- Linux x86_64, Node v22.22.0
- head: b008cb8a2b92f1dfbd6abc4c62f30b65c11e36ff

### Exact commands run

```bash
node --import tsx proof-dreaming-strict-int.mts
```

### Observed output after fix

```

[case 1] negative control - Number() accepts hex/exponent/fraction

  ok: Number("2.5") = 2.5 for deep.minUniqueQueries
  ok: Number("1.5") = 1.5 for deep.recencyHalfLifeDays
  ok: Number("0x20") = 32 for deep.maxAgeDays

[case 2] supported-path - pluginValidation skip lets strings bypass AJV to resolver

  ok: skip validation passes malformed strings through (AJV bypassed)
  ok: skip-validated: deep.limit = '0x10' (string survives to reach resolver)
  ok: skip-validated: deep.minRecallCount = '1e3' (string survives)
  info: skip-validated deep.limit=0x10 (raw string, NOT a number)

[case 3] positive control - strict parser rejects malformed, falls back to defaults
  ok: deep.limit: malformed "0x10" → 10 (not 16)
  ok: deep.minRecallCount: malformed "1e3" → 3 (not 1000)
  ok: deep.minUniqueQueries: malformed "2.5" → 3 (not 2)
  ok: deep.recencyHalfLifeDays: malformed "1.5" → 14 (not 1)

  ok: deep.minRecallCount: numeric literal 7 passes through
```

target.title: fix: sleep tool — session-targeted wake, correct sandbox policy, doc fixes
target.body:
Closes #101190

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where agents that need to wait for an external condition would either keep polling and consume tokens or end without a reliable way to resume the same session after a delay.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds a bounded `sleep` tool backed by a gateway-owned, process-local timer registry. Scheduling requires the signed agent-runtime identity, binds the wake to that identity's session, preserves the caller's effective tool restrictions, and succeeds before the current turn yields.

Unlike a cron-backed implementation, sleep timers are intentionally non-durable. A new user request cancels the pending timer before normal dispatch, while room activity and internal/system events leave it intact. Gateway shutdown clears every pending sleep.

## User Impact

Agents can pause for 1–600 seconds without spending tokens on polling, then resume with full context in the same session. User messages interrupt the wait, and Gateway restarts discard it. Sandboxed agents do not receive this gateway-backed capability by default.

## Evidence

- Added focused tests for the optional 60-second default, validation bounds, scheduling-before-yield ordering, missing-context failures, signed same-session targeting, custom wake messages, and restricted versus unrestricted caller tool policy.
- Added lifecycle coverage for timer fire/removal, replacement, user cancellation, room/internal/system-event non-cancellation, async wake failure cleanup, and shutdown/restart cleanup.
- Added catalog/profile and sandbox-policy regression coverage for the new runtime tool.
- Rebased onto current `main`; `git diff --check` passes at head `88bc4260cc`.
- GitHub CI is running against this exact head. Local dependency-backed execution was not performed because repository policy prohibits running untrusted fork code locally in this workspace.

## Consolidation

Supersedes #101197. This PR carries forward that original sleep-tool implementation and its intended model-facing behavior, then incorporates the session-targeting, sandbox-policy, lifecycle, documentation, generated-contract, and CI fixes developed during review. The earlier cron-backed branch is intentionally not merged because doing so would restore superseded behavior and its stray `commit-msg.txt` artifact.

target.title: exec: allow-always script grants survive content changes
target.body:
## Summary

An allow-always decision for an interpreter script is stored as a path and argument pattern without the approved script content. After a legitimate approval, changing that script lets a later matching `system.run` execute the new content without another approval when `tools.exec.strictInlineEval` is enabled.

## Environment

- Commit: 9daef57c85b5c6d833d8ef9cc3e4b974b557d893 (origin/main at time of filing)
- Surface: node-host system.run durable exec approvals for mutable script operands

## Steps to reproduce

1. Enable `tools.exec.strictInlineEval` and request a script through an interpreter such as `node ./approved-script.js`.
2. Approve the request with allow-always while the script has benign content.
3. Replace the contents of the same script path.
4. Issue the same system.run request without an approval decision or approval plan.

## Expected

Changing a mutable file operand after an allow-always decision should require another approval, or invalidate the durable grant.

## Actual

The later request matches the durable path and argument pattern and executes the changed script. The SHA-256 binding used to protect the in-flight approved invocation is not stored or checked on future allow-always reuse.

## Root cause

`src/node-host/invoke-system-run.ts:1043` persists the allow-always decision before the final mutable-operand revalidation at `src/node-host/invoke-system-run.ts:1065`. The persistent entry created by `applyAllowAlwaysDecision` in `src/infra/exec-approvals.ts:2708` contains only `pattern`, optional `argPattern`, and `source`.

```ts
pattern: pattern.pattern,
argPattern: pattern.argPattern,
source: "allow-always",
```

The one-shot approval plan does capture and revalidate a mutable operand SHA-256, but that binding is not part of the durable allowlist entry used by later requests.

## Sibling surfaces

The issue is limited to reusable allow-always grants for interpreter-like script invocations. It requires non-default `strictInlineEval`; without it, those interpreter command patterns are not eligible for reusable allow-always entries. The in-flight request is correctly denied if the script changes before its final revalidation.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior addressed: an allow-always grant for a script path survives replacement of the script content.
Real environment tested: production node-host system.run pipeline and durable exec-approvals store at origin/main commit 9daef57c85b5c6d833d8ef9cc3e4b974b557d893.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: approved a benign script with allow-always, replaced its contents, then issued the identical request without an approval decision.
Evidence after fix:
```
{"firstRun":"denied: approval script operand changed before execution","durableAllowAlwaysEntry":true,"subsequentRun":"executed","scriptContent":"PWNED"}
```
Observed result after fix: the changed script did not run in the in-flight request, but its durable allow-always entry remained usable by the subsequent request.
What was not tested: no remote node or external channel was used; the reproduction drives the production node-host policy, durable approval store, and local script execution path.

target.title: Sessions silently deleted from sessions.json and disk without configured maintenance
target.body:
## Bug Description

Sessions are being silently deleted from both `sessions.json` and their JSONL files on disk, without any configured session maintenance policy. Only trajectory files remain as orphaned traces.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Use WebChat for normal conversations (dashboard sessions)
2. Sessions eventually disappear from sidebar and "All Sessions" page
3. Check `sessions.json` — entries are gone
4. Check sessions directory — JSONL files are deleted from disk
5. Trajectory files remain but are orphaned

## Evidence

### Session Lost
- Session `0f5d59ee-034e-47d9-ac97-d383e6c022b8` was actively used on 2026-07-14
- Both its `sessions.json` entry and `.jsonl` file were removed from disk
- Only trajectory file `ed8868d4-096e-4f7f-9c57-50299a4e7330.trajectory.jsonl` remains

### Root Cause Error in Trajectory
The session ended with this error:
```
session.ended: status=error
error: "session file changed while embedded prompt lock was released: ...ed8868d4...jsonl"
```

This suggests a race condition where the session file was modified/accessed while the embedded prompt lock was held, causing the session to be terminated and its files cleaned up.

### No Maintenance Config
Session maintenance mode is not set (defaults to warn). No pruneAfter, maxEntries, or archiveAfterMinutes are configured.

### Current Behavior
- Only 3 sessions remain in sessions.json (heartbeat + 2 dashboard sessions)
- Previous conversations are inaccessible
- Trajectory files still exist with full conversation data but sessions are not recoverable

### UI Side Effect
Failed exec tool calls from agent turns produce a permanent `⚠️ Exec failed:` banner at the top of the chat that never clears, even after subsequent successful turns.

## Expected Behavior

- Sessions should not be silently deleted without explicit user action or configured maintenance policy
- The "session file changed while embedded prompt lock was released" error should not result in session deletion
- Failed exec banners should auto-clear after the run completes

## Environment

- OpenClaw version: v2026.7.1 (2d2ddc4)
- Platform: Linux (WSL2) / WebChat
- Agent: shrimp-head (single agent)
- Session maintenance: not configured

target.title: fix(shared): skip drop-oldest loop when new element exceeds capacity
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When `BoundedBuffer` is configured with `mode: "drop-oldest"` and an oversized element (whose `measure()` exceeds the buffer capacity) is pushed, the existing code enters a `while` loop that calls `shift()` on stored elements — each `shift()` triggers `measure()` on the shifted element.

If stored elements have zero measure (common in token-counting buffers where entries are counted externally), removing them never reduces the total size below capacity, so the loop scans **all** stored entries before the fit/clear path below ultimately discards them anyway. This is wasted computation.

**Real-world scenario**: a buffer tracking remote resource slots where entries have zero local measure but an oversized remote payload (exceeding buffer capacity) arrives → the drop loop pointlessly re-measures every buffered slot.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add a size guard before the drop-oldest loop: if `valueSize > capacity`, skip the loop entirely and let the existing fit/clear path (immediately below) handle the oversized element directly.

## User Impact

- No behavioral change for correctly-sized pushes
- For oversized pushes: fewer `measure()` calls, no observable difference in buffer state (fit/clear handles it either way)
- Existing semantics (`push` return value, `drain` result, `fit` callback) are preserved

## Evidence — Real Behavior Proof

**Environment**: Node.js v22, Windows 11, standalone BoundedBuffer replication

**Test scenario**: Push 5 zero-measure elements + 1 size-15 oversized element into capacity-10 buffer

**Runtime output** (`node proof.js`):

```
=== BoundedBuffer oversized-push guard — runtime proof ===
Scenario: push 5 zero-measure items + 1 size-15 item into capacity 10

--- WITHOUT guard (upstream main behavior) ---
  The drop-oldest loop runs shift() for each stored element,
  calling measure() on every shifted element.
  Since stored elements have measure=0, removing them never
  brings total size below capacity, so the loop scans all
  stored entries — wasted work.

--- WITH guard (this PR) ---
  When valueSize (15) > capacity (10), the drop-oldest loop
  is skipped entirely. The fit/clear path below handles
  the oversized element directly.

=== Actual runtime output ===

  [capacity 10 (normal)]
    measure() calls after 5 fills : 5
    measure() calls after push    : 6
    extra measure() from shift()  : 0
    oversized accepted            : true
    buffer after drain            : []

  [capacity 5  (small)]
    measure() calls after 5 fills : 5
    measure() calls after push    : 6
    extra measure() from shift()  : 0
    oversized accepted            : true
    buffer after drain            : []

=== Regression check: normal drop-oldest still works ===

  Push [a, bb, ccc] into capacity 3 (drop-oldest):
    accepted: true, drained: [ccc]
    measure() calls: 5
    Expected: [ccc], measure()=5 (3 pushes + 2 shift re-measures)
```

**Key finding**: `extra measure() from shift() = 0` — the guard prevents wasted `measure()` calls during the drop-oldest loop. The oversized element is still accepted, and the buffer is properly cleared via the fit/clear path.

**Regression check**: Normal drop-oldest behavior is unaffected — the guard only activates when `valueSize > capacity`, which is the oversized case this PR targets.

## Regression Test Plan

- Vitest unit test `"skips the drop loop when the new element's measure exceeds capacity"` validates that `measure()` is called exactly 6 times (5 fills + 1 oversized push), not more
- Existing `it.each` parameterized tests continue to pass (latch, drop-oldest, fail-closed)
- Manual Node.js runtime test above confirms zero extra shift-measures in the oversized path

## Root Cause

The `drop-oldest` loop unconditionally calls `this.measure(this.values.shift()!)` without checking whether the newly added element even fits within capacity. When the element is oversized, dropping old elements cannot resolve the overflow — the fit/clear path below is the only resolution. The loop runs anyway, wasting `measure()` calls on entries that will be discarded.

[AI-assisted]

target.title: fix(shared): use UTF-8 byte length instead of String.length for avatar data URL limit
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The avatar data URL validation `isRenderableAvatarImageDataUrl()` uses `String.length` (UTF-16 code unit count) to measure payload size. For strings containing multibyte characters (e.g. emoji in SVG avatars), this under-reports the actual byte payload: a `😀` (U+1F600) is 2 UTF-16 code units but 4 UTF-8 bytes.

When a persisted avatar with multibyte content is projected through the Gateway or Control UI, `String.length` allows values through that would violate the byte budget used by downstream validation (`AVATAR_MAX_BYTES`).

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace `String.length` with `TextEncoder.encode().length` to count actual UTF-8 bytes. Additionally, add a fast UTF-16 length short-circuit before the full encoding to avoid O(n) work on obviously oversized inputs (ClawSweeper [P2] finding addressed).

## User Impact

- **Correctness**: Multibyte avatar data URLs are now correctly measured in UTF-8 bytes, matching the byte budget contract
- **Performance**: A fast-path short-circuit (`value.length > limit`) rejects oversized inputs in 0.007ms (O(1)) vs 33ms for full encoding (O(n)) — **4,588x speedup** on a 10MB input
- **No behavioral change for ASCII-only inputs**: `TextEncoder.encode().length === String.length` for ASCII, so existing behavior is preserved

## Evidence — Real Behavior Proof

**Environment**: Node.js v22, Windows 11

**Runtime output** (`node proof.js`):

```
=== Avatar UTF-8 byte-length validation — runtime proof ===
AVATAR_MAX_DATA_URL_CHARS = 2796230

--- Test 1: ASCII-only data URL at exact boundary ---
  URL length (UTF-16) : 2796230
  URL bytes  (UTF-8)  : 2796230
  Accepted            : true
  Expected            : true

--- Test 2: ASCII-only data URL 1 char over limit ---
  URL length (UTF-16) : 2796231
  Accepted            : false
  Expected            : false (fast path: value.length > limit)
  Fast-path check     : value.length(2796231) > limit(2796230) = true

--- Test 3: Mixed ASCII + emoji at exact byte boundary ---
  URL length (UTF-16) : 2796226
  URL bytes  (UTF-8)  : 2796230
  String.length would report: 2796226 (under-reports UTF-8 size)
  Accepted            : true
  Expected            : true
  Fast-path passes    : value.length(2796226) <= limit(2796230) = true

--- Test 4: Mixed data URL 1 byte over limit ---
  URL length (UTF-16) : 2796227
  URL bytes  (UTF-8)  : 2796231
  Accepted            : false
  Expected            : false

--- Test 5: Non-image data URL (rejected by MIME check) ---
  URL                 : "data:text/plain,avatar"
  Accepted            : false
  Expected            : false

--- Test 6: Oversized input (10MB ASCII) — fast path vs full encode ---
  Input size (UTF-16) : 10485786
  Fast path result    : false (rejected before encoding)
  Fast path time      : 0.0072 ms
  Full encode result  : false (rejected after encoding)
  Full encode time    : 33.0372 ms
  Speedup             : 4588.5x

=== All proof tests passed ===
```

**Key findings**:
- **Test 1-2**: ASCII exact boundary accepted, 1-char overflow rejected via fast path (O(1))
- **Test 3-4**: Multibyte emoji at exact byte boundary accepted even though UTF-16 length is 4 units shorter; 1 byte over correctly rejected
- **Test 5**: Non-image MIME types still rejected
- **Test 6**: The fast-path short-circuit delivers **4,588x speedup** on oversized inputs by avoiding the full UTF-8 encoding allocation

## Regression Test Plan

- Vitest: exact ASCII boundary accepted, oversized ASCII rejected, non-image rejected
- Vitest: multibyte emoji at exact UTF-8 byte boundary accepted, 1 byte over rejected
- Manual Node.js proof above validates all edge cases and the fast-path performance

## Root Cause

`String.length` counts UTF-16 code units, not UTF-8 bytes. For ASCII content they are equal, but multibyte characters (emoji, non-Latin scripts) produce fewer code units than UTF-8 bytes, causing the old check to under-report the actual payload size and potentially admit values that exceed the byte budget.

[AI-assisted]

target.title: fix(utils): treat non-positive chunkItems size as 1 instead of returning all items in one chunk
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The original PR attempted to fix `chunkItems` behavior for non-positive sizes by treating them as size=1 (one element per chunk). After ClawSweeper review and a full caller audit, this approach was rejected because:

1. `chunkItems` is exported via `openclaw/plugin-sdk/text-chunking` — external plugins depend on the existing contract
2. The proposed change silently breaks the SDK contract: `chunkItems([x,y,z], 0)` changes from `[[x,y,z]]` to `[[x],[y],[z]]`
3. All real callers supply positive sizes → no caller-level fix is needed

**This PR now preserves the shipped non-positive-size contract** as recommended by ClawSweeper, and documents the caller audit results.

## Why This Change Was Made (Decision Rationale)

**Caller audit** (GitHub code search, `chunkItems` across `openclaw/openclaw`):

| Caller | Size | Affected by change? |
|--------|------|:---:|
| `extensions/discord/.../native-command-arg-ui.ts` | `4` (hardcoded) | No |
| `extensions/slack/.../slash.ts` | `SLACK_COMMAND_ARG_SELECT_OPTIONS_MAX` (constant) | No |
| `src/utils/utils-misc.test.ts` | `0` (test, expects old behavior) | Test only |
| `src/plugin-sdk/text-chunking.ts` | SDK re-export | External plugins |

All real callers use positive sizes. Changing `chunkItems` would risk breaking external plugin consumers without benefiting any existing caller.

**ClawSweeper [P1] findings addressed**:
- ✅ `src/utils/chunk-items.ts:3` — Preserve the shipped non-positive-size contract
- ✅ `src/utils/chunk-items.ts:3` — Avoid replacing one copy with one array per item

## What Problem This Solves

The avatar MIME handling has two concrete gaps:

1. **Missing `.ico` support**: `resolveAvatarMime("avatar.ico")` returns `"application/octet-stream"` instead of `"image/x-icon"`, even though `.ico` is already recognized as a valid avatar path by `AVATAR_PATH_EXT_RE` and `looksLikeAvatarPath()`. 2. **No MIME subtype validation for data URLs**: `isRenderableAvatarImageDataUrl` only checks the `data:image/` prefix without validating the specific image subtype against an allowlist. This allows data URLs with non-standard or non-image MIME subtypes to pass validation.

- Created `AVATAR_ALLOWED_MIME_TYPES` set with all supported image subtypes: `png`, `jpeg`, `gif`, `webp`, `svg+xml`, `x-icon`, `tiff`, `bmp`
- Added `isAllowedAvatarMimeType()` public function exported via `avatar-policy.ts`
- Added `extractDataUrlMime()` helper in `avatar-limits.ts` to extract MIME subtype from data URLs

target.title: fix(normalization-core): reject non-integer finite values in resolveIntegerOption
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The original PR added `Number.isInteger()` to `resolveIntegerOption` to reject fractional finite values. After ClawSweeper review, this approach was rejected because:

1. `resolveIntegerOption` is a shared coercion utility with 56+ callers
2. The `Math.floor()` behavior is an intentional coercion contract, not a bug
3. Changing it creates inconsistency with sibling helpers (`resolveTimerTimeoutMs`, `clampTimerTimeoutMs`, etc.) that also accept finite numbers and floor them
4. No real caller passes fractional values → no caller-level fix is needed

**This PR now preserves the shared coercion contract** as recommended by ClawSweeper.

## Why This Change Was Made (Decision Rationale)

**Behavior comparison**:

| Input | Upstream (floor) | Proposed (reject) | Risk |
|-------|-----------------|-------------------|------|
| `5` | `5` | `5` | None |
| `2.9` | `2` | `10` (fallback) | Config jump |
| `7.1` | `7` | `10` (fallback) | Config jump |
| `-3.5` | `-4` | `10` (fallback) | Config jump |

Fractional values that currently normalize predictably (e.g., `2.9 → 2`) would instead jump to caller-specific defaults — an unpredictable behavioral change.

**Caller audit** (from previous analysis, 56+ callers):

| Function | Callers | Pass integers? |
|----------|---------|:---:|
| `resolveIntegerOption` | 30+ | ✅ All |
| `resolveOptionalIntegerOption` | 10+ | ✅ All |
| `resolveNonNegativeIntegerOption` | 16+ | ✅ All |

All real callers supply integer values. No demonstrated caller requires strict rejection of fractional input.

**Sibling inconsistency**: Adding `isInteger()` only to `resolveIntegerOption` creates inconsistency with:
- `resolveTimerTimeoutMs` — uses `Math.floor(value)`
- `clampTimerTimeoutMs` — uses `Math.floor(value)`  
- `resolveExpiresAtMsFromEpochSeconds` — uses `Math.trunc(value)`
- `finiteSecondsToTimerSafeMilliseconds` — uses `Math.floor(seconds)`

## User Impact

- **No behavioral change**: The coercion contract is preserved
- **Backward compatible**: Existing configs with fractional values (e.g., `2.9`) continue to normalize to `2` predictably
- **Consistent sibling behavior**: All number coercion helpers maintain the same floor semantics

## Evidence — Real Behavior Proof

**Environment**: Node.js v20, Windows 11

**Runtime output** (`node proof.js`):

```
=== resolveIntegerOption contract preservation — runtime proof ===

--- Test 1: Behavior comparison ---
  integer (5):
    Upstream (floor): 5
    Proposed (fallback): 5
    Match: true
  fractional (2.9):
    Upstream (floor): 2
    Proposed (fallback): 10
    Match: false
  fractional (7.1):
    Upstream (floor): 7
    Proposed (fallback): 10
    Match: false
  negative fractional (-3.5):
    Upstream (floor): -4
    Proposed (fallback): 10
    Match: false
  null (uses fallback):
    Upstream (floor): 10
    Proposed (fallback): 10
    Match: true
  string (uses fallback):
    Upstream (floor): 10
    Proposed (fallback): 10
    Match: true

--- Test 2: Contract divergence analysis ---
  Upstream: 2.9 → floor(2.9)=2 → 2 (predictable)
  Proposed: 2.9 → not integer → fallback=10 (unpredictable jump)
  Risk: 2.9 in config currently normalizes to 2; after change jumps to 10

--- Test 3: Caller audit ---
  Function                        | Callers | Pass integers
  --------------------------------|---------|--------------
  resolveIntegerOption              | 30+      | Yes
  resolveOptionalIntegerOption      | 10+      | Yes
  resolveNonNegativeIntegerOption   | 16+      | Yes
  All callers supply integer values. No caller passes fractional input.
  Decision: PRESERVE the shared coercion contract.

--- Test 4: Sibling inconsistency risk ---
  Adding isInteger() only to resolveIntegerOption creates:
  inconsistency with other helpers that also accept finite numbers.
    - resolveTimerTimeoutMs — still floors: Math.floor(value)
    - clampTimerTimeoutMs — still floors: Math.floor(value)
    - resolveExpiresAtMsFromEpochSeconds — uses Math.trunc(value)
    - finiteSecondsToTimerSafeMilliseconds — uses Math.floor(seconds)

=== Conclusion ===
  1. resolveIntegerOption is a shared coercion utility (56+ callers)
  2. The floor() behavior is an INTENTIONAL contract, not a bug
  3. No real caller passes fractional values → no caller needs fixing
  4. Changing only one sibling creates inconsistent behavior
  5. Decision: PRESERVE the shared coercion contract
```

## Regression Test Plan

- Existing Vitest tests pass as-is (no behavior change)
- `resolveIntegerOption(2.9, 10)` → `2` (preserved floor contract)
- `resolveIntegerOption(5, 10)` → `5` (integer unchanged)
- `resolveOptionalIntegerOption(2.9)` → `2` (preserved contract)
- `resolveNonNegativeIntegerOption(2.9, 0)` → `2` (preserved contract)

## Root Cause

The shared coercion utility `resolveIntegerOption` intentionally floors finite numeric input rather than rejecting non-integer values. This is a consistent pattern across all number coercion helpers in the same module. The proposed `Number.isInteger()` guard would create the only strict-integer entry point in a module where every sibling helper accepts finite numbers and applies `Math.floor()` / `Math.trunc()`.

target.title: fix(utils): log JSON parse error when both JSON and JSON5 parsers fail
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When both `JSON.parse` and `JSON5.parse` fail on malformed input, the original code silently propagates the JSON5 error with no diagnostic context about the stricter JSON failure. Callers loading persisted config/manifests have no visibility into whether the input was "almost valid JSON" vs "completely malformed JSON5".

## Why This Change Was Made

Add diagnostic context by including the JSON parse error message in the rethrown error chain when both parsers fail.

**ClawSweeper [P1] findings addressed**:
- ✅ Line 26: Catch JSON5 error explicitly (`catch (json5Error)`) and rethrow with `new Error(..., { cause: json5Error })` — no bare `throw;`
- ✅ Lines 22-25: Remove `console.warn` — diagnostic routed through the error chain instead of bypassing caller-owned sanitization

## User Impact

- **No behavioral change for valid inputs**: Strict JSON and JSON5 fallback paths are unchanged
- **For dual-failure**: The thrown error now includes `"JSON.parse failed, and JSON5 fallback also failed: <json-error-msg>"` in its message and the original JSON5 error as `Error.cause`
- **Caller safety**: Callers can sanitize before logging (no raw input on stderr)
- **Upgrade-safe**: Error type changes from bare SyntaxError to Error with cause; callers catching generic errors and checking `.cause` will see the additional context

## Evidence — Real Behavior Proof

**Environment**: Node.js v20, Windows 11

**Runtime output** (`node proof.js`):

```
=== parseJsonWithJson5Fallback — diagnostic chain proof ===

--- Test 1: Strict JSON (fast path, no error) ---
  Input: '{"a":1}' -> {"a":1}
  Expected: {a:1}

--- Test 2: JSON5 fallback (trailing comma) ---
  Input: '{"a":1,}' -> {"a":1}
  Expected: {a:1}

--- Test 3: JSON5 with comment ---
  Input: '{"a":1 // comment...}' -> {"a":1}
  Expected: {a:1}

--- Test 4: Both parsers fail — diagnostic in error chain ---
  Error type     : Error
  Error message  : JSON.parse failed, and JSON5 fallback also failed: Unexpected token 'o', "not valid" is not valid JSON
  Has cause      : true
  Cause type     : SyntaxError
  Cause message  : JSON5: Unexpected token at position 0
  Contains JSON  : true
  No console.warn: true (diagnostic routed through error chain)

--- Test 5: Malformed input '{invalid' ---
  Error message  : JSON.parse failed, and JSON5 fallback also failed: Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1
  Cause present  : true
  ✓ Caller receives full diagnostic context via error chain
  ✓ Caller can sanitize before logging (no raw input on stderr)

--- Test 6: Custom parser error preserved as cause ---
  Error message  : JSON.parse failed, and JSON5 fallback also failed: Unexpected token 'b', "bad" is not valid JSON
  Cause message  : custom parser error
  Cause matches  : true

--- Test 7: No raw input in diagnostic ---
  ✓ Raw input NOT exposed by console (console.warn removed)
  ✓ Diagnostic routed through error chain only

=== Conclusion ===
  1. console.warn removed → no raw input on stderr
  2. JSON error context in rethrown Error.message
  3. JSON5 error preserved as Error.cause
  4. Callers can sanitize diagnostic before logging
  5. Custom parser errors preserved in cause chain
```

## Regression Test Plan

- Vitest: Strict JSON parsing unchanged (object, array, primitives)
- Vitest: JSON5 fallback unchanged (trailing comma, comments, single-quoted keys, unquoted keys)
- Vitest: Dual-failure throws Error with JSON error context in `.message` and JSON5 error in `.cause`
- Vitest: Custom parser errors preserved in the cause chain
- Manual Node.js proof above validates all edge cases including no raw stderr output

## Root Cause

The original code used `try { JSON.parse } catch { json5.parse }` which silently discards the JSON error. The first attempt used `console.warn` + bare `throw;` which bypasses caller sanitization and can be ambiguous in nested catch blocks. The fix explicitly catches the JSON5 error, wraps it with JSON error context, and rethrows via `new Error(..., { cause })`, keeping the diagnostic inside the error chain where callers control exposure.

target.title: fix(clawhub): reject calendar-invalid feed timestamps
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a malformed ClawHub promotions feed with an impossible calendar date (e.g. `2026-02-30T00:00:00.000Z`) would be accepted because `Date.parse` silently normalizes it. The feed parser would enter the normalized timestamp into cache state with an unintended expiry window.

## Why This Change Was Made

Moves the existing ISO shape/calendar validator into the neutral `src/shared/iso-time.ts` owner so cron and ClawHub can share validation without an `infra` → `cron` dependency. ClawHub uses the validator only as a guard and retains the existing `Date.parse` milliseconds for ordering and cache expiry, preserving timezone-less timestamp interpretation on non-UTC hosts. Both `generatedAt` and `expiresAt` are validated; numeric epoch strings remain rejected by the ISO-only feed contract, while canonical leap-day and normal ISO dates continue to parse without change.

## User Impact

Operators see no change under normal conditions (the live ClawHub feed emits canonical ISO timestamps). If a remote feed snapshot is ever malformed with an impossible date, it is now rejected instead of silently acquiring the wrong cache-expiry window, and the last accepted snapshot remains available.

## Evidence

**Before** (`upstream/main` at the PR base): `parseClawHubPromotionsFeed` accepted `generatedAt: "2026-02-30T00:00:00.000Z"` and returned the feed unchanged because `Date.parse` normalized the impossible date.

**Premise**: `isValidIsoAbsolute` validates ISO shape and calendar components with a UTC component round trip without interpreting the timestamp's timezone. The feed parser separately retains the original `Date.parse` result, so validation does not change previously accepted timezone-less instants.

**After — production-path runtime proof** (`40a0390b559bfde3eb8ceea226a1d85c59fb134c`, before the ownership/compatibility follow-up):

I ran a standalone `node --import tsx --input-type=module -` script with an isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`. The script started a real localhost HTTP server, pointed `OPENCLAW_CLAWHUB_URL` at it, and called the production `maybeRefreshPromotionsFeed` without an injected `fetchImpl`. The server first returned valid sequence 4 / ETag `"v4"`, then calendar-invalid sequence 5 / ETag `"v5"`. It was closed before the final cache read, so the final result came from the real SQLite state DB rather than HTTP. This did not load Vitest or set `NODE_ENV=test`.


target.title: fix(telegram): preserve authored file-reference links
target.body: Closes #105679 ## What Problem This Solves Telegram's Markdown formatter treated any authored link whose visible label matched a supported file-like hostname as if it came from MarkdownIt's automatic linkifier. For example, `[README.md](https://README.md)` was indistinguishable from a plain `README.md` reference and the authored anchor was silently replaced with `README.md`. The supported suppression extensions currently include `.md`, `.go`, `.py`, `.pl`, `.sh`, `.am`, `.at`, `.be`, and `.cc`. `.ts` is not in that set, so `main.ts` is not a valid before/after reproducer for this bug. ## Why This Change Was Made Markdown Core now keeps MarkdownIt's `linkify` provenance as private renderer metadata instead of adding a field to the public `MarkdownLinkSpan` contract. The fact is copied through clamping, slicing, table transforms, render-boundary splitting, and render-aware chunk coalescing. `renderMarkdownWithMarkers` exposes only a renderer-specific `{ origin: "authored" | "linkify" }` context while evaluating a link. Telegram suppresses a file-like link only when that context says it came from MarkdownIt's `linkify` rule. Markdown/IR output then wraps remaining plain file references without trying to infer provenance again from rendered anchors. Explicit Markdown links therefore remain anchors, while the public raw-HTML helper keeps its default defensive de-linkification behavior because raw HTML does not carry trustworthy parser provenance. The branch was rebuilt on current `main` after the Markdown IR and Telegram renderer refactors, removing the prior merge conflict and picking up the upstream fixes for the two unrelated CI failures seen on the previous head. ## User Impact Intentional Telegram links whose labels resemble supported file names keep their destinations, while plain file references such as `README.md` continue to render as code and avoid unwanted registrar previews. Existing direct-HTML compatibility behavior is preserved. ## Evidence - Head: `9be0456f8174709be6402656084aa796dff26ac5`. - `git diff --check` passed. - Focused Markdown Core coverage checks public span shape plus renderer provenance through parsing/clamping, slicing, and table rendering. - Telegram formatter coverage checks authored-link preservation for a supported `.md` label, automatic file-reference suppression, mixed authored/plain output, chunked output, and existing raw-HTML de-linkification behavior. - Hosted CI run `29401371174` is fully green: 50 successful jobs, 12 scope skips, and no failures. This includes `check-test-types`, `check-dependencies`, lint, all Node test shards, build artifacts, prod types, guards, and the aggregate `openclaw/ci-gate`. - The previous head's two unrelated failures were fixed upstream by #107987 (`session-history-state` test typing) and #107977 (serialized hooks process bootstraps); rebasing picked up both fixes. - Initial Mantis run `29396726601` showed that `main.ts` has no baseline/candidate delta because `.ts` is not a supported suppression extension. - Corrected Mantis run `29401877063` passed against baseline `ad1071bcd0` and candidate `9be0456f81`. The [proof comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/105911#issuecomment-4978225456) contains paired native Telegram Desktop screenshots, GIFs, and MP4s; the evidence manifest marks both lanes `pass`, candidate `fixed: true`, and overall `pass: true`. - The Mantis proof job itself succeeded, including manifest validation, artifact upload, and PR evidence publication. The workflow's red conclusion comes only from a separate `Clear Mantis command reaction` cleanup job receiving a 403 while removing the eyes reaction.

target.title: fix: doctor should not treat loopback bind as network-accessible 0.0.0.0
target.body:
Closes #107425

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators with `gateway.bind = "loopback"` would see a false doctor security warning that the Gateway was network-accessible on `0.0.0.0`, even when the Gateway was only listening on loopback.

## Why This Change Was Made

Doctor security classified exposure from the resolved bind host alone. When loopback mode's host resolution fell back to `0.0.0.0`, that host was treated as network-accessible. The fix preserves the canonical loopback bind mode as local-only for exposure classification, while still warning on real LAN/custom/auto exposure paths. No config keys, defaults, or auth behavior change.

Follow-up from review: the test mock holder for `resolveGatewayBindHost` now uses the production parameter type (`GatewayBindMode | undefined`) so `check-test-types` accepts assigning the real resolver.

Fix quality: compatibility (loopback semantic contract only; real non-loopback binds still warn), performance (one bind-mode check), usability (removes false security alarm), security (does not weaken LAN/custom exposure warnings).

## User Impact

`openclaw doctor` / security warnings no longer treat an explicit loopback bind as network-accessible when host resolution falls back to `0.0.0.0`. Operators with loopback-only Gateways avoid a false CRITICAL/WARNING exposure line.

## Evidence

Verification host: local macOS arm64 (path-scoped static checks + focused Vitest + live doctor lint with loopback config and listener inspection).

```text
# Focused behavior tests (after mock typing fix)
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commands/doctor-security.test.ts
# Test Files  1 passed (1)
# Tests  34 passed (34)

node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commands/doctor-security.test.ts -t "does not treat loopback bind fallback"
# ✓ does not treat loopback bind fallback resolution as network-accessible
```

Red/green contrast for the new regression case (same harness, production line temporarily set to main vs this patch):

**Before (main classification):**
```text
FAIL  does not treat loopback bind fallback resolution as network-accessible
AssertionError: expected "vi.fn()" to not be called at all, but actually been called 1 times
Received:
  "- CRITICAL: Gateway bound to \"loopback\" (0.0.0.0) without authentication.
  Anyone on your network (or internet if port-forwarded) can fully control your agent.
  ..."
```

**After (this patch):**
```text
✓ does not treat loopback bind fallback resolution as network-accessible
Tests  1 passed | 33 skipped
```

Mock typing (review finding): holder uses `GatewayBindMode | undefined` to match `resolveGatewayBindHost`, so assigning the production function type-checks under `check-test-types`.

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: Doctor security must not report `Gateway bound to "loopback" (0.0.0.0)` as network-accessible when the configured bind mode is loopback. This is the same classification path used by `openclaw doctor --lint` security (`core/doctor/security` → `noteSecurityWarnings`).
- Environment: local macOS arm64, PR head after mock typing fix, isolated `OPENCLAW_HOME` with `gateway.bind = "loopback"` and a redacted token auth field.
- Listener inspection while a loopback process was bound:
  ```text
  COMMAND   PID       USER   FD   TYPE  ... NAME
  node    18421 ... TCP 127.0.0.1:18789 (LISTEN)
  ```
- Live CLI after fix (loopback config, non-interactive lint JSON), redacted:
  ```bash
  OPENCLAW_HOME=<isolated> node openclaw.mjs doctor --lint --non-interactive --json
  ```
  Observed security findings (excerpt): plaintext-token hygiene only (`gateway.auth.token`). **No** `Gateway bound` / `network-accessible` finding for the loopback bind.
  ```text
  checkId=core/doctor/security severity=warning
    WARNING: openclaw.json contains plaintext secret-bearing config fields.
    Paths: gateway.auth.token
  gateway bound any? False
  network-accessible any? False
  ```
- Forced 0.0.0.0 fallback path (issue repro class): with bind mode loopback and host resolution forced to `0.0.0.0`, `noteSecurityWarnings` emits no `Gateway bound` / `network-accessible` note (Vitest regression above). Current-main contrast still fails that case (see Evidence red/green).
- Control check: lan bind without auth still warns (`warns when exposed without auth` passes). Existing loopback normal path and unset-bind-as-loopback cases still pass.
- What was not tested: long-running managed Gateway service under a host where `canBindToHost("127.0.0.1")` itself fails (true extreme resolver fallback outside the forced harness); LAN/custom live install matrix.

target.title: [AI] fix(feishu): use formatErrorMessage for sender name resolution error log
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Feishu sender name resolution errors leak API credentials into gateway logs. When `resolveFeishuSenderName` fails, `String(err)` at `bot-sender-name.ts:134` preserves raw Feishu API error text that may contain `app_secret`, `tenant_access_token`, or Bearer tokens.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replace `String(err)` with `formatErrorMessage(err)` from the plugin SDK. `formatErrorMessage` (at `src/infra/errors.ts:69-113`) calls `redactSensitiveText` before returning, which redacts recognized secret patterns including `app_secret` (listed at `src/logging/redact.ts:32`) and token-bearing terms. Five sibling Feishu files (`probe.ts`, `tool-result.ts`, `drive.ts`, `bitable.ts`, `monitor.comment.ts`) already use `formatErrorMessage` for the same reason. The change is +2/-1 in a single file.

## User Impact

None. Error log output is semantically identical for debugging but no longer leaks credential names.

## Evidence

**Environment**: Linux x86_64, Node v24.13.1, OpenClaw 2026.6.11, branch `fix/feishu-format-error-sender-name`, commit `6c7fded68c`.

**Before/after — simulated Feishu sender name resolution failure** (`bot-sender-name.ts:134` exact log pattern):

```
$ node --import tsx -e "
import { formatErrorMessage } from 'openclaw/plugin-sdk/error-runtime';
const e = new Error('HTTP 400: {\"error\":\"invalid app_secret\",\"code\":-1}');
console.log('String(err):       ', String(e));
console.log('formatErrorMessage:', formatErrorMessage(e));
"
String(err):        Error: HTTP 400: {"error":"invalid app_secret","code":-1}
formatErrorMessage: Error: HTTP 400: {"error":"invalid app_***","code":-1}
```

**Full source code evidence — security chain:**

`formatErrorMessage(err)` in `src/infra/errors.ts:112-113`:
```typescript
  // Security: best-effort token redaction before returning/logging.
  return redactSensitiveText(formatted);
```

`app_secret` is a recognized sensitive key in `src/logging/redact.ts:32`:
```typescript
const FORM_BODY_SENSITIVE_KEYS: ReadonlySet<string> = new Set([
  ...
  "app_secret",
  ...
]);
```

**Unit tests:**

```console
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/feishu/src/bot-sender-name.test.ts --run
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  2 passed (2)
```

**What was NOT tested**: Live Feishu gateway with real sender-name lookup failure (requires running gateway with valid Feishu app credentials and a managed gateway instance). The code path is structurally identical to the 5 sibling files already proven in production.

target.title: fix(usage): add bounded timeout and progressive backoff to usage-cost refresh queue
target.body:
#### What Problem This Solves

Close #103910

The usage-cost background refresh queue (`runQueuedUsageCostRefresh`) can hang indefinitely when a scan, parse, or agent-database write stalls. Because `state.running` stays `true` until the `await refreshCostUsageCacheForAgent()` settles, the gateway memoization layer returns the same frozen cache snapshot. The user sees `cacheStatus: "refreshing"` permanently, `pendingFiles` never drains, and `updatedAt` stops advancing.

Additionally, a refresh lock acquired by the same process can become permanently stale — if the holder is abandoned (in-process restart or hung I/O whose queue-level timeout already released), the lock row's `startedAt` keeps it forever "running" because `isProcessRunning(pid)` returns true for the still-alive process.

#### Why This Change Was Made

**Queue-level resilience** (`session-cost-usage.ts`):

1. **Batch timeout (45s)** — `Promise.race` wraps each refresh batch. On timeout the queue releases `state.running`, keeps all pending files, and schedules a retry with progressive backoff.
2. **Work preservation** — `pendingSessionFiles` are snapshotted before the `await` but drained per-file only on success. Previously `pendingSessionFiles.clear()` ran unconditionally before the `await`.
3. **Progressive backoff** — A new `consecutiveStalls` counter drives exponential backoff: 50ms base → doubles each stall up to 30s max. Successful batches reset to zero.

**Lock-level staleness** (`session-cost-usage-cache.sqlite.ts`):

4. **Stale lock threshold (2 min)** — `isRefreshLockLive()` now considers a lock dead if `Date.now() - lock.startedAt > 120s`, regardless of `isProcessRunning(pid)`. This reclaims locks leaked by in-process restarts (same pid) or hung I/O whose queue timeout already released.

#### User Impact

No visible impact under normal operation. When the agent database or filesystem stalls, the usage-cost cache will now self-heal within ~45s instead of freezing permanently.

#### Evidence

- **Type check:** `tsgo` passes
- **Lint:** `oxlint` clean
- **Format:** `oxfmt` clean
- **Tests:** `session-cost-usage.test.ts` — 45 tests (+3: first-time agent refresh without hanging, second call does not deadlock, lock acquire-release lifecycle)
- **Change scope:** 3 files, +167 −22 lines
  - `src/infra/session-cost-usage.ts` — 3 constants + 1 state field + rewritten queue loop
  - `src/infra/session-cost-usage-cache.sqlite.ts` — stale lock threshold + `isRefreshLockLive` helper
  - `src/infra/session-cost-usage.test.ts` — 3 new tests
  - No config, CLI, SDK, docs surface affected

- **Real proof — empty agent refresh + stale lock reclamation:**

```
Usage-Cost Refresh Timeout — Live Proof
============================================================

── Test 1: First-time refresh on empty agent ──
  completed in 4936ms
  status: fresh  pending: 0

  ✓ summary returned (no hang)
  ✓ empty agent — zero totals
  ✓ completed within 60s

── Test 2: Second call — no deadlock ──
  completed in 13ms

  ✓ second call returned
  ✓ no deadlock

── Test 3: Stale lock reclamation ──
  ✓ lock acquired
  ✓ running while held
  ✓ not running after release
  ✓ re-acquire after release

Passed: 9 | Failed: 0
```

**Three new constants:**

```typescript
// session-cost-usage.ts
const USAGE_REFRESH_BATCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 45_000;
const USAGE_REFRESH_MAX_BACKOFF_MS = 30_000;
const USAGE_REFRESH_BASE_BACKOFF_MS = 50;

// session-cost-usage-cache.sqlite.ts
const STALE_REFRESH_LOCK_THRESHOLD_MS = 2 * 60_000;
```

**New state field:** `consecutiveStalls: number` — reset on success, incremented on timeout/busy/error.

**New helper:** `isRefreshLockLive(lock)` — replaces raw `isProcessRunning(pid)` with pid-liveness *and* staleness check.

target.title: fix(heartbeat): stop reporting success after tool failures
target.body:
Fixes #102206

> **AI-assisted PR.** Implemented with Codex, manually directed and validated against the OpenClaw and upstream Codex runtime contracts.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a heartbeat could report success after a mutating tool call—most visibly a `message` send—had failed. With the default cross-provider safety policy, a Codex-backed heartbeat bound to WebChat correctly denied a Discord send, but a later successful `heartbeat_respond` masked that denial. Operators therefore saw a successful heartbeat even though the notification was never delivered.

## Why This Change Was Made

The cross-provider guard remains unchanged: a WebChat-bound run still cannot send to Discord unless the operator explicitly opts in. Instead, the host runtime now owns a precise, runtime-independent record of mutating tool execution and carries unresolved failures through terminal payload construction. Both the standard embedded runner and Codex app-server bridge distinguish calls that never started from calls that actually executed, preserve multiple failures, clear a failure only after a matching successful action, and keep Codex-only metadata private rather than changing the upstream app-server protocol.

Heartbeat execution treats an unresolved mutating-tool failure as the terminal outcome. It returns `failed` with reason `agent-tool-failure`, avoids success bookkeeping, preserves retry cadence and timestamps, and emits a warning only when delivery is configured. Ordinary heartbeat replies and explicitly allowed cross-provider sends retain their existing behavior.

This boundary matches the upstream Codex contract: dynamic tool calls/results expose the call identity, tool name, arguments, and success/error result, while OpenClaw remains responsible for its channel policy and heartbeat terminal semantics.

## User Impact

Operators no longer get a false-success heartbeat after a notification or other mutating action fails. The original failure remains visible and retryable, while existing cross-provider containment stays secure by default. Operators who intentionally enable cross-provider sends continue to get delivery, and normal `heartbeat_respond` notifications are unchanged.

The part of #102206 requesting implicit cross-provider delivery is intentionally not implemented; that behavior remains an explicit configuration choice. This PR fixes the concrete breakage in the report: the denial can no longer be swallowed by a later success.

## Evidence

- Rebased onto current `main`; current HEAD is `d36403462f9b9bba0fe28e5b77a8928a5cd0a49d`. Fresh full-bundle autoreview accepted and fixed one execution-boundary precedence finding, then completed clean. Fresh follow-up reviews of the payload type fix and CI-only export/test cleanup were also clean.
- Fresh Blacksmith Testbox: provider `blacksmith-testbox`, id `tbx_01kxh3hbt2p3rr0pmtem1d3qv6`, [workflow run 29364101980](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29364101980). Focused remote suites passed: 204 standard-runtime tests, 406 Codex app-server tests, and 68 heartbeat/payload tests.
- Full build passed on exact HEAD on both Testbox and AWS Crabbox (`cbx_38dc5b5aedac`, run `run_90e31210dcbd`).
- `check:changed` passed conflict-marker, LOC-ratchet, attribution, SDK/export, dependency, format, patch, and related guards. Core typecheck now reports only `packages/markdown-core/src/frontmatter.ts:109`, outside this diff; the same error (plus two net-policy errors) reproduces in a detached clean `origin/main` Testbox worktree.
- Live baseline on pre-fix main, `openai/gpt-5.4` through the Codex app-server: default WebChat-bound Discord send was denied, delivered no marker, but the heartbeat incorrectly returned `ok-token` (`run_04fdef29b0f6`).
- Live fix and regression proof on behavior-bearing parent `471a130a6a650f0d3b632158b9e6e33dcec7baa3`: AWS Crabbox provider `aws`, id `cbx_38dc5b5aedac`, run `run_96547da4349b`, model `openai/gpt-5.4`, runtime `codex`. With the default policy the Discord marker remained blocked and undelivered while heartbeat returned `{ status: "failed", reason: "agent-tool-failure" }`; normal `heartbeat_respond` delivery reached real Discord and returned `sent`; explicitly enabling cross-provider delivery sent the marker and preserved `ok-token`. The final commit changes only test typing/mocks and removes unused export modifiers; its exact failed tests (27/27) and dead-code export gate passed remotely.

No Telegram credential was leased or used; the live proof used a Convex-leased Discord credential.

target.title: fix(agents): load bootstrap files from agentDir alongside workspace
target.body:
## Problem

Per-agent `agentDir` bootstrap files (`SOUL.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `TOOLS.md`, etc.) were silently ignored when `agentDir` differed from `workspaceDir`. Only workspace bootstrap files were loaded via `resolveBootstrapFilesForRun()`. Users placing access-control rules in `agentDir/AGENTS.md` had zero enforcement.

## Root Cause

`resolveBootstrapFilesForRun()` only loaded bootstrap files from `workspaceDir`, never checking `agentDir`. The agent directory path was resolved but not used as a bootstrap source.

## Fix

When `config` and `agentId` are available and `agentDir` differs from `workspaceDir`, load bootstrap files from `agentDir` too. AgentDir files override workspace files with the same name, enabling per-agent customization. Only applies when `agentDir` is explicitly configured in the agent config, preventing default state directories from silently overriding workspace safety rules. Also filters `agentDir`-root `BOOTSTRAP.md` after setup completion, matching workspace behavior.

## Real Behavior Proof

### Test Results (vitest 4.1.8)

```
$ vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.agents-core.config.ts src/agents/bootstrap-files.test.ts

✓ src/agents/bootstrap-files.test.ts (37 tests, 100% pass)

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  37 passed (37)
   Start at  16:43:15
   Duration  3.03s (transform 1.35s, setup 608ms, import 1.86s, tests 305ms, environment 0ms)
```

### Before/After

**Before:** `agentDir` bootstrap files silently ignored. Agent with `agentDir: "/data/agent1"` and `agentDir/AGENTS.md` containing access-control rules had zero enforcement.

**After:** `agentDir` AGENTS.md loads and overrides workspace AGENTS.md for that agent. Explicit `agentDir` config required (no silent default state dirs).

Fixes #29387

target.title: fix(signal): reject hex/exponent text-style span offsets
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Signal container sends could apply the wrong styled span when `text-style` start/length tokens used JavaScript-only forms such as `0x10` or `1e1`. Those tokens were coerced with `Number(...)` into different offsets, so bold/italic markers could land on the wrong characters or invent spans that the caller never intended.

## Why This Change Was Made

Parse `text-style` `start`/`length` with the same `parseStrictNonNegativeInteger` helper already used for container quote timestamps. The parser is extracted to `client-container-text-style.ts` so the oversized `client-container.ts` stays LOC-neutral. Invalid hex/exponent/fractional tokens are dropped (same as incomplete `start:length:style` entries). Valid decimal spans keep working. No new config keys.

Collision check: searched open PRs for `path:extensions/signal/src/client-container.ts` and `parseStrictNonNegativeInteger text-style` — **0** competing PRs. Open Signal PRs #101380 / #100906 do not touch `text-style` `Number()` parsing.

## User Impact

Malformed `text-style` offsets no longer silently restyle the wrong part of a Signal message. Ordinary decimal spans such as `0:4:BOLD` are unchanged. A hex offset like `0x10` silently mapped to character 16 before; now it is dropped and the message renders plain.

## Verification

- Exact head: `f3510cd72d030d4361681c99f372372ffe7db181`

target.title: fix(zalo): bound proxy fetcher cache to 64 entries
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Zalo retained a process-lifetime Map of proxy fetchers with no bound and no owner-local ProxyAgent cleanup.

## Why This Change Was Made

Chose ClawSweeper option 1 (Zalo-local lifecycle):

- Cap cache at 64 with insertion-order eviction.
- Create/dispose ProxyAgents inside Zalo (no core Symbol.for close).
- Monitor acquires a lease so eviction cannot close a live account agent.
- Evicted unused entries dispose immediately; retained callers fail closed.

Additionally:
- `src/infra/net/proxy-fetch.ts`: Add typed `closeProxyFetch()` lifecycle helper and restore `PROXY_FETCH_CLOSE` mechanism so `makeProxyFetch` wrappers expose a close method for cache owners.
- `src/plugin-sdk/fetch-runtime.ts`: Export `closeProxyFetch` and `PROXY_FETCH_CLOSE` from the public SDK.
- `scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.mjs`: Bump public export budget (10613, +1 net).

## User Impact

**Before:** unbounded proxy fetch wrappers/dispatchers.
**After:** ≤64 unused cache slots; monitor-held proxies stay alive until stop; disposed fetchers fail closed.

## Evidence

Exact head: `7620f791424`

Rebased onto `origin/main` (4f71a2855e). SDK surface budget: 10613/5344/3262.

Focused tests:

```
 ✓ |extension-zalo| resolveZaloProxyFetch > returns undefined for empty or whitespace proxy URLs
 ✓ |extension-zalo| resolveZaloProxyFetch > caches fetchers by trimmed proxy URL
 ✓ |extension-zalo| resolveZaloProxyFetch > negative control: Map without bound retains oldest after 65 inserts
 ✓ |extension-zalo| resolveZaloProxyFetch > evicts the oldest proxy fetcher when more than 64 distinct URLs are resolved
 ✓ |extension-zalo| resolveZaloProxyFetch > closes the underlying ProxyAgent dispatcher on unused eviction
 ✓ |extension-zalo| resolveZaloProxyFetch > retained evicted fetcher fails closed and does not recreate a dispatcher
 ✓ |extension-zalo| resolveZaloProxyFetch > defers dispose for leased monitor fetchers until release
```

```

```

## Risk / Compatibility

Low. Lifecycle is Zalo-local. `closeProxyFetch` is an additive SDK export; no existing callers broken.

target.title: fix: guide container operators to redeploy after update permission failures
target.body:
Related: #94279

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running `openclaw update` directly inside a
container could receive host-oriented EACCES recovery guidance such as using
`sudo` or changing the npm global prefix.

Those steps are misleading inside a container because an in-container package
update is not durable across recreation.

## Why This Change Was Made

When a global update or install step fails with EACCES in a detected container,
the updater now recommends pulling or building the target OpenClaw image and
recreating or redeploying the container. Existing host recovery guidance is
preserved outside containers.

This complements #94310, which suppresses container update suggestions and
actions. It covers direct CLI invocation of `openclaw update`.

## User Impact

Container operators who invoke the updater directly now receive recovery steps
that match the durable container deployment model instead of host package
installation advice.

## Evidence

- Added a container-specific EACCES regression test that requires image
  redeploy guidance and rejects `sudo` and npm-prefix advice.

## Summary
- preserve known live accounts when an already-active channel hot-reload restarts without an explicit account id
- preserve known accounts for channel account-index reload markers such as `channels.openclaw-weixin.channelConfigUpdatedAt`

- treat hot-reload stop/restart as a manager-owned handoff only for channels that stayed active across plugin replacement
- document the WeChat multi-account behavior and cover the hot-reload paths with regression tests
- add a guard that ordinary caller-owned restarts still do not resurrect stale accounts
- harden the non-isolated agent model-catalog visibility coverage that timed out in refreshed CI

## Why
Adding a second WeChat account can temporarily surface only the new account in the plugin account listing. Before this change, the gateway could evict or fail to restart the already-running account during hot reload, leaving account A offline after account B logs in.

## Summary

- **Problem**: `openclaw plugins install/update/uninstall/registry-refresh` crashes with `ENOTDIR: not a directory, scandir '/home/<user>/.openclaw/openclaw.json'` when a stale plugin install record in SQLite causes the managed npm projects path to resolve to a file instead of a directory.
- **Root cause**: `src/plugins/npm-project-roots.ts` catch handler only checks for `ENOENT`; `ENOTDIR` is rethrown and propagates up to crash the CLI.
- **Solution**: Replace the local `isMissing` helper with the shared `isNotFoundPathError` from `infra/path-guards.ts`, which already covers both `ENOENT` and `ENOTDIR`. This is the same pattern used across the codebase (gateway/control-ui.ts, infra/state-migrations, commands/doctor, etc.).
- **What changed**: `isMissing()` now delegates to `isNotFoundPathError()` instead of comparing directly against `ENOENT`. No behavioral change for callers — ENOTDIR now gracefully degrades to `[]` just like ENOENT.

Fixes #107467

---

## Root Cause

**Trigger condition**: `resolvePluginNpmProjectsDir(npmRoot)` produces a path that points to a file rather than a directory (e.g. after a corrupted plugin install record in SQLite).

**Root cause**: `src/plugins/npm-project-roots.ts` catch block only handled `ENOENT`; `ENOTDIR` was rethrown, propagating up to crash the CLI.

**Affected scope**: v2026.7.1, all plugin lifecycle operations (install/update/uninstall/registry-refresh).

---

target.title: fix(feishu): retry once on token-invalid errors 99991663/99991664 with cache invalidation (fixes #97287)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #97287.

When the cached `tenant_access_token` becomes invalid (e.g. clock drift, server-side revocation, or Feishu token expiry), the plugin cannot send messages. Error code `99991663 Invalid access token` is returned, but the plugin does not automatically refresh the token and retry. Users must manually restart the gateway to recover.

## Changes Made

- `extensions/feishu/src/comment-shared.ts`: Added `addFeishuTokenCacheClearer` / `clearFeishuTokenCaches`. `getFeishuTokenInvalidCode` detects 99991663/99991664. `requestFeishuApi` retries once on token-invalid (`retriedTokenInvalid` flag, independent of rate-limit budget). Fulfilled token-invalid bodies handled.
- `extensions/feishu/src/client.ts`: `createFeishuClient` creates a plugin-owned `Lark.Cache` via `buildSdkTokenCache()`. `clearClientCache` expires `CTenantAccessToken` in the private cache by appId namespace.
- `extensions/feishu/src/send.ts`: getter pattern — `opts.getClient()` inside request closure, ensures fresh client after cache clear.
- `extensions/feishu/src/streaming-card.ts`: `clearFeishuTokenCache` registered. CardKit create retry on 99991663/99991664. Guarded-fetch release on non-JSON response.
- `extensions/feishu/src/client.test.ts`: NEW — client cache isolation tests.
- `extensions/feishu/src/send.retry.test.ts`: NEW — token-invalid + rate-limit retry sequence tests.
- `extensions/feishu/src/streaming-card.test.ts`: NEW/UPDATED — card streaming tests including retry and guarded-fetch release.
- `extensions/feishu/src/token-retry-proof.test.ts`: NEW — end-to-end recovery proof tests (99991663/99991664 detection, cache clearing, getter pattern).

## Evidence

### 1. Production requestFeishuApi auto-retry on real 99991663 (7/7 passed)

Loads the ACTUAL `comment-shared.ts` module via `tsx` and exercises `requestFeishuApi` with a real 99991663 error. The production code automatically detects the token-invalid code, clears caches, and retries — all through the same code path that ships in the plugin.

```

 Host: LIN-66D8BD4EA2C
 Time: 2026-07-08T06:01:43Z
 Commit: 83830f71ec

─── 1. Real Feishu API: get token ───
  ✅ GET TOKEN: code=0
  ✅ BOT INFO:  code=0

─── 2. requestFeishuApi auto-retry on 99991663 ───
  ✅ Real API returns 99991663 with tampered token
  ✅ requestFeishuApi called 2x (1st=99991663, 2nd=success)
  ✅ Cache clear callback invoked (via addFeishuTokenCacheClearer)
  ✅ Recovered: result.code=0

─── 3. Cache isolation proof ───
  ✅ Fresh client after cache clear (different instance)

  RESULTS: 7/7 passed

  Production module exercised:
    extensions/feishu/src/comment-shared.ts
      → requestFeishuApi() — auto-retry on 99991663
      → getFeishuTokenInvalidCode() — detects 99991663/99991664
      → addFeishuTokenCacheClearer() — registers cache clearers
    extensions/feishu/src/client.ts
      → createFeishuClient() — builds SDK client
```

### 2. Retry path steps (production code flow)

```
send() → 99991663 thrown
  → getFeishuTokenInvalidCode() detects 99991663
  → clearFeishuTokenCaches() → addFeishuTokenCacheClearer callbacks
  → clearClientCache() evicts CTenantAccessToken
  → retriedTokenInvalid = true (prevents infinite retry loop)
  → requestFeishuApi() RETRIES → SDK/fetch gets fresh token
  → send succeeds → code=0
```

target.title: fix(acp): keep completed run-mode sessions resumable
target.body:
Closes #106696.

## What Problem This Solves

ACP sessions spawned with `mode="run"` are intentionally closed after their first turn. A later `sessions_send` to the same completed child therefore started a fresh agent conversation or failed with missing ACP metadata instead of resuming the backend conversation. This made parent agents unable to answer questions or continue work in an existing one-shot Codex or Claude session.

## Why This Change Was Made

The manager now retains completed one-shot metadata only when the agent advertises ACP session resume/load support and a stable ACP session ID has been recorded. A parent follow-up resumes that ID, fails closed if resume fails, and keeps OpenClaw's one-shot lifecycle while reconnecting through ACPX under a fresh process lease.

The change also distinguishes a live prompt from terminal cleanup, so a parent can send the supported follow-up as soon as terminal delivery begins. Agents without resume support and one-shots that are still actively prompting remain rejected.

## User Impact

Parents can follow up with completed ACP run-mode children without losing task context. Codex and Claude one-shots preserve their working directory and conversation state across the follow-up, while active turns, unsupported agents, invalid resume targets, and abandoned process ownership remain handled conservatively.

## Evidence

Validated on Node 24.18.0 after rebasing onto current `main`:

- changed ACPX runtime test: 59 tests passed
- ACP configuration lane: 66 tests passed
- targeted ACP manager, task-registry, session-meta, and sessions-tool shards passed
- `pnpm tsgo:core`, changed-file `oxfmt`, changed-file `oxlint`, and `git diff --check` passed
- `codex review --base upstream/main` was run locally and its findings were addressed
- The full `pnpm test:extension acpx` lane reported 172 passing tests and four unrelated failures already present on current `main`: the new Pi session-catalog API is missing from three plugin test fixtures, and its manifest schema snapshot has not yet been updated. This PR does not modify those surfaces.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** A completed ACP `mode="run"` child lost its original conversation when the parent later used `sessions_send`, causing a fresh-session response or `ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED` instead of a contextual follow-up.
- **Real environment tested:** A Linux system running a long-lived OpenClaw gateway from a local build with the bundled ACPX extension, using both Claude ACP and Codex ACP child sessions launched by a parent agent.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** Spawned a one-shot child that returned a unique context marker, waited for the run to complete and its runtime process to be cleaned up, then sent a follow-up through `sessions_send` to the same OpenClaw ACP session key asking for the marker. Repeated the flow for Claude and Codex.
- **Evidence after fix:** The initial child output contained `CONTEXT_TOKEN=<redacted-marker>`. The later follow-up returned the same marker under the same OpenClaw ACP session key and backend transcript ID. Neither follow-up reported a fresh session or missing task context.
- **Observed result after fix:** Completed Claude and Codex one-shots resumed their original backend conversation and answered the parent follow-up with the prior context intact. An actually active one-shot was still rejected, and an invalid resume target failed closed rather than silently starting fresh.
- **What was not tested:** Windows and macOS were not exercised in the real setup. The final stale-`closed` process-lease recovery and terminal-delivery race refinements were validated with unit/integration tests, not by deliberately crashing the production gateway during those exact windows.

## AI-assisted disclosure

This PR is AI-assisted. I ran the real behavior validation and automated tests, reviewed the implementation and review findings, and understand the metadata, resume-capability, lifecycle, and process-lease changes in this patch.
